one_liner: GPT-2 greedy inference in about 900 lines of Fortran on vendor sgemm; HF transformers/PyTorch takes 4-16% longer on M1 Max.
what_it_does: Runs GPT-2 inference (124M to 1558M weights) from a fastGPT-specific GGUF file: gpt2.f90 holds the model and the generate() loop, tokenizer.f90 a BPE encoder/decoder, driver.f90 the model loader, and there are two programs, gpt2 (reads an `input` namelist file) and chat. Only greedy decoding is supported; there is no sampling, batching or training. It is a standalone Fortran program and module API, not a replacement for the transformers pipeline() interface.
how_it_is_fast: Every matmul (QKV projection, per-head K^T Q and V*softmax, output projection, MLP, logits) is a cblas_sgemm call on column-major float32 arrays, through Accelerate on macOS or OpenBLAS when chosen. Layer norm, softmax, GELU and embedding are plain Fortran array loops built with -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -funroll-loops. Decoding uses a KV cache, so after the prompt prefill each step pushes one token through. Because PyTorch calls the same BLAS, the measured edge is the missing Python interpreter, HF generate() bookkeeping and per-op dispatch, plus a near-instant model load (raw float32 arrays read straight from the file). The README's fastest row also uses an optional polynomial fast_tanh inside GELU.
when_to_use: You want a small, readable GPT-2 inference reference you can vendor into a Fortran or HPC code base (MIT license, no Python at run time).
Short one-shot prompts from scripts where startup dominates: the README's total-run row is 0.401 s for fastGPT against 4.867 s for PyTorch, almost all of it Python imports and model loading.
Apple Silicon with Accelerate, a single sequence, greedy decoding and tens of tokens, which is the setup the README benchmarks.
Compiler or language work that needs a realistic, self-checking Fortran workload: CI builds it with gfortran and LFortran 0.60.0 and checks generated tokens against reference arrays.
when_not_to_use: Any model other than GPT-2, or anything needing top-k, top-p, temperature sampling, batching, quantised weights or training. None of these is implemented (issues #7 and #8 are open).

Long generations or throughput serving: main copies the whole KV cache on every token, runs attention heads serially (issue #2 open) and spends most of its BLAS time packing operands. PR #88 measures main at 14.95 tok/s for 20 tokens and 10.92 tok/s for 1000 tokens on one i5-1235U core, and its unmerged fixes report 2.75-4.09x.
Multi-core OpenBLAS without the KV cache: by the README's own table, PyTorch is faster at 2, 4 and 8 cores.
Output that must match HF tokenization for arbitrary text: the pre-tokenizer splits only on space, comma and period, not on GPT-2's regex.
Production embedding: generate() always prints each token to stdout, errors end the process with error stop, context is capped at n_ctx 1024, and the ifort segfault (issue #14) is still open.

integration.form: source-drop (CMake builds a static library `fastgpt` plus the gpt2 and chat executables; there is also an fpm package)
integration.dependencies: gfortran; for speed, a BLAS: Accelerate (macOS default) or OpenBLAS (-DFASTGPT_BLAS=OpenBLAS), plus an OpenMP runtime for the timer. The default elsewhere is Fortran intrinsic matmul. Pre-converted GGUF weights download from huggingface.co/certik/fastGPT. Converting weights yourself needs Python 3.9, TensorFlow 2.11 and gguf-py from llama.cpp commit 4e9a7f7.
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.13; gfortran (CI pins 14.2.0 on macOS, version unpinned on Ubuntu) or LFortran 0.60.0; ifort is broken (issue #14)
integration.platforms: macOS (Accelerate, tested on Apple M1 Max) and Linux (OpenBLAS or intrinsic matmul); CI runs on macos-latest and ubuntu-latest. Release flags use -march=native, so binaries are not portable.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; generate() takes the model as intent(in) and keeps its KV cache local, but it writes to stdout. The only parallelism is inside BLAS.

gotchas: Harness flaw: the fast_tanh rows (0.288 s, and the 0.401 s total run) cannot be rebuilt from the source as shipped. gpt2.f90 defines fast_tanh, but gelu() calls the intrinsic tanh. Open issue #25 shows that fast_tanh changes the last 9 of 100 greedy tokens on the 1558M model, so those rows do not compute the same output as PyTorch.

Harness flaw: the timed regions differ. fastGPT's 'Running model' timer leaves out its own tokenizer, while pt.py times the whole pipeline() call, HF tokenization included. The README's example run prints 0.074 s encoding plus 0.304 s generation, 0.378 s, which is slower than PyTorch's 0.346 s (derived from page data). The PyTorch (Accelerate) row came from a conda-forge PyTorch that only ran after libcblas.3.dylib was symlinked over libopenblas.0.dylib (issue #26, PyTorch version unrecorded); none of that setup is in the repo.

The default builds have no BLAS and a dead timer. The fpm build and the non-Apple CMake default (FASTGPT_BLAS=Fortran) link linalg_f.f90 (intrinsic matmul) and omp_dummy.f90, whose omp_get_wtime returns 0, so the run prints 'Time: 0.000s' and the speed ratio divides by zero. build.sh calls encode_input.py at the repo root, but that file now lives only in comparison/.

generate() allocates and copies the whole KV cache in and out on every token: 2 x n_embd x 2 x n_layer x 4 bytes, about 147 KB per cached position for 124M, so the cost grows quadratically with length. The chat stop-text check slices output_txt from len-len('User:')+1, which is below 1 while the reply is shorter than 5 characters (an out-of-bounds substring that -fcheck=all Debug builds will trap).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick fastGPT over llama2.zig, llama2.mojo or llm.mojo when you need GPT-2 weights or Fortran specifically. Those siblings run Llama-2 or GPT-2 training and are measured against llama2.c/llm.c at -O3, a tighter C baseline than this entry's Python-driven PyTorch.
verified_claims_summary: On an Apple M1 Max, GPT-2 124M generated 20 greedy tokens from a 19-token prompt with a KV cache in 0.299 s with fastGPT (gfortran, Accelerate sgemm) against 0.346 s for an HF transformers 4.26.1 pipeline on PyTorch (version unrecorded) with Accelerate, about 1.16x. With OpenBLAS at 1-8 cores PyTorch takes 4-16% longer, and without the cache PyTorch wins at 2, 4 and 8 cores (ratios derived from page data). Both sides call the same vendor sgemm, so the gap measures Python and HF dispatch overhead plus fastGPT's timer leaving out its own tokenizer, not Fortran code generation.
status_note: Active but slow-moving (last commit 2026-02-14, mostly CI and LFortran upkeep; PR #88's reported 2.75-4.09x speedup has been open since March 2026 without a maintainer benchmark), MIT and small enough to vendor, but the README table dates from March 2023, before the GGUF loader, the Fortran tokenizer and the 2026 allocation changes, and it rests on harness flaws: fast_tanh rows that need a source edit and change the output (issue #25), a PyTorch Accelerate row from a symlinked conda BLAS (issue #26), a fastGPT timer that leaves out its 0.074 s tokenizer while pt.py's includes HF tokenization, and pt.py hard-coding OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 for the multi-core rows.
